entries.avoid: Do not call ordinary data augmentation active perception.
examples: The task requires active perception because the agent must move to reveal {occluded or unobserved information}.
Actions affect both {task progress} and the observations available for future decisions.
entries.expression: active perception
entries.guidance: Describe the action-dependent sensing process and whether actions are chosen explicitly for information gain or jointly for task reward.
entries.meaning: Perception in which an agent's actions influence which observations become available, coupling information acquisition with control.

provenance.note: Independent synthesis of linked primary sources; no source sentence copied.

entries.avoid: Do not claim cross-embodiment generalization when every evaluated robot appears in training under the same interface.
examples: We evaluate cross-embodiment transfer by adapting the pretrained policy to {held-out robot} with {amount of data}.
The embodiments differ in {morphology, camera setup, and action space}.
entries.expression: cross-embodiment transfer
entries.guidance: State whether transfer is zero-shot, requires fine-tuning, or only shares pretraining. Reserve 'generalization' for a held-out evaluation that directly supports it.
entries.meaning: The application or adaptation of learned knowledge across robots or agents with different morphologies, sensors, action spaces, or control interfaces.

provenance.note: Independent synthesis of linked primary sources; no source sentence copied.

entries.avoid: Do not describe any stochastic policy as a diffusion policy.
examples: The diffusion policy generates an action sequence conditioned on {observation history}.
At inference, we execute {action horizon} actions from each denoised sequence before replanning.
entries.expression: diffusion policy / action diffusion
entries.guidance: Specify the predicted horizon, conditioning observations, diffusion parameterization, sampling steps, and how generated actions are executed.
entries.meaning: A policy that represents a conditional distribution over actions or action sequences through a denoising diffusion process.

provenance.note: Independent synthesis of linked primary sources; no source sentence copied.

entries.avoid: Do not use domain randomization as a generic label for ordinary image augmentation or claim coverage of the real domain without evaluation.
examples: During simulation training, we randomize {textures, lighting, camera, dynamics, or latency} over {specified ranges}.
Domain randomization exposes the policy to {variation} before real-world deployment.
entries.expression: domain randomization
entries.guidance: List randomized parameters and distributions, and separate visual randomization from dynamics randomization. Whether the real domain lies within effective support is an empirical question.
entries.meaning: Training over deliberately varied simulation parameters to make a model robust across a distribution intended to cover or bracket variability encountered in the real system.

provenance.note: Independent synthesis of linked primary sources; no source sentence copied.

entries.avoid: Do not use 'embodied' for a passive model that only processes a fixed image or text dataset without an interaction formulation.
examples: We study embodied AI agents that perceive {sensory inputs} and act through {action space} in {environment}.
The agent's observations depend on its previous actions, creating a closed perception–action loop.
entries.expression: embodied AI
entries.guidance: Specify the body, sensors, action space, environment, and task. For simulated agents, state which physical or interaction constraints are modeled.
entries.meaning: The study of agents that perceive and act within an environment, where their observations, actions, and learning are shaped by embodiment and closed-loop interaction.

provenance.note: Independent synthesis of linked primary sources; no source sentence copied.

entries.avoid: Do not call a policy generalist solely because one architecture is reused across several separately trained tasks.
examples: We train a generalist robot policy on {tasks, environments, and embodiments}.
We separately evaluate in-distribution multi-task performance and transfer to {new setting}.
entries.expression: generalist robot policy
entries.guidance: State the diversity actually represented in training and evaluation. Distinguish multi-task performance, zero-shot generalization, and fine-tuning ability.
entries.meaning: A policy trained across diverse tasks, environments, or robot data with the aim of supporting multiple behaviors and transfer beyond a single narrowly trained task.

provenance.note: Independent synthesis of linked primary sources; no source sentence copied.

entries.avoid: Do not claim zero-shot sim-to-real if any real-world fine-tuning or calibration materially updates the policy.
examples: We evaluate zero-shot sim-to-real transfer by deploying the simulation-trained policy without {real-world policy updates}.
The transfer gap arises from mismatches in {appearance, dynamics, sensing, or actuation}.
entries.expression: simulation-to-real (sim-to-real) transfer
entries.guidance: Name what transfers, what is randomized or adapted, the real-world evaluation, and whether real data is used before deployment.
entries.meaning: Training or developing a model in simulation and deploying or adapting it to a physical system whose observations or dynamics differ from the simulator.

provenance.note: Independent synthesis of linked primary sources; no source sentence copied.

entries.avoid: Do not call a pipeline visuomotor if vision only labels a dataset and is unavailable to the deployed controller.
examples: The visuomotor policy maps {image history and proprioception} to {action chunk}.
We train the policy end to end from {visual input} to {robot command}.
entries.expression: visuomotor policy
entries.guidance: Specify visual inputs, auxiliary conditioning, action representation, control frequency, and whether perception and control are trained end to end.
entries.meaning: A policy that maps visual observations, often together with proprioception or goals, to motor actions or action sequences.

provenance.note: Independent synthesis of linked primary sources; no source sentence copied.

entries.avoid: Do not group methods only by architecture when their data and deployment assumptions dominate the comparison.
examples: We organize prior work by its supervision signal, whether training uses online interaction, and the sensory information available at deployment.
Unlike methods trained on {data regime}, our approach assumes {different verified regime}.
entries.expression: Embodied methods should be positioned by supervision, interaction regime, and deployment assumptions.
entries.guidance: Use concrete axes such as demonstrations versus rewards, simulation versus real data, online versus offline collection, and privileged versus deployable observations.
entries.meaning: Structures embodied-AI related work around how data is obtained, whether learning is interactive, and what information or hardware is available at deployment.

provenance.note: Independent synthesis of linked primary sources; example wording is original.

entries.avoid: Do not use embodiment as a synonym for environment or task.
examples: The policy is evaluated on embodiments that differ in {morphology, sensors, or action space}.
We encode embodiment-specific {proprioceptive or action information}.
entries.expression: embodiment
entries.guidance: Name the aspects that differ across embodiments—camera placement, morphology, control frequency, action coordinates, or dynamics—rather than using the term abstractly.
entries.meaning: The agent-specific physical or simulated form that determines its sensing, actuation, kinematics, and interaction constraints.

provenance.note: Canonical term indexed from linked primary papers; examples are original.

entries.avoid: Do not use the two terms as universally interchangeable when the algorithm is not direct supervised cloning.
examples: We use behavioral cloning to fit the policy to demonstration state–action pairs.
The method belongs to imitation learning but differs from behavioral cloning in {interactive or distributional mechanism}.
entries.expression: imitation learning versus behavioral cloning
entries.guidance: Use behavioral cloning for the supervised objective and imitation learning for the wider family, which may include interactive data collection, occupancy matching, or other objectives.
entries.meaning: Imitation learning is the broader problem of learning behavior from demonstrations, while behavioral cloning usually denotes direct supervised prediction of expert actions from observations.

provenance.note: Independent synthesis of linked primary sources; no source sentence copied.

entries.avoid: Do not replace the phrase with an equally vague adjective such as 'strong generalizability.'
examples: We evaluate generalization to unseen {objects} and robustness to {perturbation}.
The policy succeeds under {specified shift} in {fraction} of trials.
entries.expression: generalization ability / robustness ability
entries.guidance: Prefer 'generalization to {held-out condition}', 'robustness to {perturbation}', or the exact measured outcome. 'Capability' is acceptable only when its scope is stated.
entries.meaning: These noun stacks often conceal the evaluated shift or perturbation and can sound like literal translations rather than operational claims.

provenance.note: Original anti-pattern guidance authored for this repository.

entries.avoid: Do not intensify inherently comparative or absolute adjectives.
examples: {method} outperforms {baseline} on {metric} in {setting}.
entries.expression: more superior / more optimal
entries.guidance: Use 'outperforms' for a verified metric comparison, 'is more effective' with a criterion, or simply report the numbers.
entries.meaning: Redundant comparative forms that obscure the actual comparison dimension.

provenance.note: Original anti-pattern guidance authored for this repository.

entries.avoid: Avoid 'perform good', 'gets a good result', and comparison without a metric or baseline.
examples: {method} achieves higher {metric} than {baseline} under {protocol}.
entries.expression: perform good / get better performance
entries.guidance: Use 'performs well' only for an informal summary; in papers, prefer 'achieves higher {metric}' or a quantified comparison.
entries.meaning: Non-idiomatic or underspecified performance wording often produced by literal translation.

provenance.note: Original anti-pattern guidance authored for this repository.

entries.avoid: Do not infer interaction from unrelated single-drop variants or unmatched optimization settings.
examples: The joint variant changes {metric} by {value}, compared with {individual effects}, suggesting an interaction between {components}.
The benefit of {component A} appears only with {component B}, consistent with their intended coupling.
entries.expression: The joint variant differs from the sum of individual changes, suggesting an interaction between {components}.
entries.guidance: Use only when the factorial variants and common reference permit the comparison. Quantify the observed non-additivity and uncertainty.
entries.meaning: Describes non-additive ablation behavior as evidence consistent with a component interaction.

provenance.note: Original results-analysis pattern authored after the section-writing audit.

entries.avoid: Do not conclude that a component is necessary in every setting from one ablation.
examples: Removing {component} reduces {metric} from {a} to {b}, indicating that it contributes to {capability} in {setting}.
entries.expression: Removing {component} reduces {metric}, indicating that {bounded interpretation}.
entries.guidance: Report the size and uncertainty where possible. 'Indicating' should introduce a bounded interpretation rather than a causal universal.
entries.meaning: Connects an ablation result to a component-level interpretation.

provenance.note: Original reusable pattern authored for this repository.

entries.avoid: Avoid replacing the constraint with 'limited performance' or implying that every prior method has the same weakness.
examples: For {task}, existing methods remain limited by {assumption} when {condition}.
In {setting}, current approaches require {resource or supervision}, which restricts {capability}.
entries.expression: For {task}, existing methods remain limited by {specific constraint}.
entries.guidance: Use only after verifying that the closest relevant methods share the stated constraint. Name the setting in which it matters.
entries.meaning: Introduces a concrete research gap tied to a task and a named constraint.

provenance.note: Original section-aware pattern authored after the section-writing audit.

entries.avoid: Do not use 'key insight' for a restatement of the method name or an unsupported causal story.
examples: Our key insight is that {representation property} permits {operation}, which enables {capability}.
The central observation is that {condition}; this motivates {design choice}.
entries.expression: Our key insight is that {insight}, which enables {capability}.
entries.guidance: Express a technical relationship that the paper actually establishes or uses. Follow with the mechanism that realizes it.
entries.meaning: States the conceptual observation that motivates the method and connects it to a scoped capability.

provenance.note: Original section-aware pattern authored after the section-writing audit.

entries.avoid: Avoid chaining several modules with 'novel' adjectives without explaining their function.
examples: We introduce {method}, which combines {mechanisms} to {objective}.
We develop {method}, a {method class} that {mechanism} for {task}.
entries.expression: We introduce {method}, which {mechanism} to {objective}.
entries.guidance: Replace the slots with the paper-level mechanism, not a list of low-level implementation details. Use the exact method name from the manuscript.
entries.meaning: Names the contribution and summarizes its operative mechanism and objective in one sentence.

provenance.note: Original section-aware pattern authored after the section-writing audit.

entries.avoid: Do not average incompatible tasks or select the largest favorable result while implying it summarizes the full study.
examples: Across {number} {tasks}, {method} improves {metric} by {value} percentage points over {comparator}.
Under {shift}, {method} reduces {error metric} from {baseline value} to {method value}.
entries.expression: Across {evaluation scope}, {method} changes {metric} by {value} relative to {comparator}.
entries.guidance: Specify whether the value is absolute, relative, or in percentage points. Use the same aggregation and comparison set as the referenced display.
entries.meaning: Reports one principal verified result with its evaluation scope, metric, magnitude, and comparator.

provenance.note: Original section-aware pattern authored after the section-writing audit.

entries.avoid: Avoid turning benchmark evidence into an unrestricted claim about real-world deployment or general intelligence.
examples: These results support {conclusion} for {task family} under {protocol}.
The evidence supports transfer across {held-out axis}, but does not establish {broader scope}.
entries.expression: These results support {scoped conclusion} under {evaluated conditions}.
entries.guidance: Name the datasets, tasks, shifts, assumptions, or system conditions that bound the conclusion when they are material.
entries.meaning: Closes an empirical summary with a conclusion bounded by the actual evaluation.

provenance.note: Original section-aware pattern authored after the section-writing audit.

entries.avoid: Do not mix rerun and copied numbers without labeling their provenance and compatibility.
examples: Baseline results are reproduced using the authors' {release} with {documented changes}.
Results marked with {symbol} are taken from {verified source}; all others are rerun under our protocol.
entries.expression: Baseline results are {rerun or sourced} using {implementation and version}.
entries.guidance: State code commit or release, consequential changes, tuning policy, and whether the reported protocol matches the present evaluation.
entries.meaning: Records whether baseline numbers were reproduced or taken from a source and identifies the implementation.

provenance.note: Original experimental-writing pattern authored after the section-writing audit.

entries.avoid: Do not claim a matched ablation when variants use different data, budgets, selection, or evaluation.
examples: Ablation of {components} with all variants trained under the same {data and compute budget}. Values report {statistic} over {seeds}.
Component analysis on {task}; the full model is {row}, and each variant changes {factor}.
entries.expression: Ablation of {components} with all variants trained under {matched protocol}.
entries.guidance: Define component indicators, full-model row, metric, runs, uncertainty, and any retuning policy in the remaining caption.
entries.meaning: Introduces an ablation caption and states the matched condition needed to compare variants.

provenance.note: Original table-caption pattern authored after the section-writing audit.

entries.avoid: Do not label a table efficiency when it reports only parameter count or latency without task quality.
examples: Quality and deployment cost measured on {hardware} at {precision} and batch size {value}. Latency includes {boundary}.
Task success and control latency under {deployment protocol}; values report {statistic} over {repeats}.
entries.expression: Quality and deployment cost measured under {hardware and timing protocol}.
entries.guidance: Name hardware, precision, batch, input, warm-up, timing boundary, repeats, resource units, and metric directions.
entries.meaning: Frames an efficiency caption around both outcome quality and a reproducibly measured deployment resource.

provenance.note: Original table-caption pattern authored after the section-writing audit.

entries.avoid: Do not use 'unseen' without specifying what was withheld and whether it influenced model selection.
examples: Generalization from {training environments} to held-out {environments}. Test environments are excluded from training and validation.
Transfer from {embodiments} to unseen {embodiments}; success rates are averaged over {trials}.
entries.expression: Generalization from {training condition} to {held-out condition}.
entries.guidance: Continue with the held-out unit, selection protocol, metrics, runs, uncertainty, and reference condition.
entries.meaning: Names the training and held-out conditions at the start of a generalization-table caption.

provenance.note: Original table-caption pattern authored after the section-writing audit.

entries.avoid: Do not use a one-phrase caption that forces readers to reconstruct the protocol from the prose.
examples: Results on {tasks} under the {split} protocol. Higher {metric} is better; values are {units} and report {statistic} over {runs}.
Evaluation on {environment} with {budget}. Lower {metric} is better, and bold marks the best comparable result.
entries.expression: Results on {dataset or task} under {protocol}. {Metric direction and units}.
entries.guidance: Continue with aggregation, uncertainty, runs, emphasis, and protocol exceptions. Use the exact split and evaluation setting.
entries.meaning: Provides the first two functional sentences of a self-contained main-results caption.

provenance.note: Original table-caption pattern authored after the section-writing audit.

entries.avoid: Do not show only values near the chosen optimum or imply a scaling law from a narrow sweep.
examples: Sensitivity to {parameter}; the dagger denotes the validation-selected configuration. All other settings and seeds are fixed.
Scaling with {data or model size}; bold identifies the configuration used for the main experiments, not an oracle test optimum.
entries.expression: Sensitivity to {parameter}; {default marker} denotes the selected configuration.
entries.guidance: State the full range, selection data and objective, fixed factors, runs, uncertainty, and changed resource when scale varies.
entries.meaning: Introduces a sensitivity caption and identifies the configuration used elsewhere in the paper.

provenance.note: Original table-caption pattern authored after the section-writing audit.

entries.avoid: Do not write 'the gains are due to' without an identifying intervention.
examples: These results are consistent with the hypothesis that {component or inductive bias} improves {measured behavior}.
entries.expression: These results are consistent with the hypothesis that {mechanism}.
entries.guidance: Use when evidence supports but does not isolate the proposed explanation. Follow with an ablation or limitation if available.
entries.meaning: Links observations to a mechanism without claiming that the experiment identifies causality.

provenance.note: Original reusable pattern authored for this repository.

entries.avoid: Do not compare your full method with one isolated weakness of a baseline.
examples: Unlike {method family}, which relies on {assumption}, our approach {mechanism without that assumption}.
entries.expression: Unlike {comparison class}, which {defining behavior}, our approach {distinct behavior}.
entries.guidance: Keep the grammatical comparison parallel and verify that the characterization holds for the cited comparison class.
entries.meaning: Contrasts two methods on one explicit mechanism or assumption.

provenance.note: Original reusable pattern authored for this repository.

entries.avoid: Do not use 'novel' as a substitute for explaining what is contributed.
examples: Our main contribution is {method or analysis} that {capability} under {evaluated conditions}.
entries.expression: Our main contribution is {artifact or insight} that {verified capability}.
entries.guidance: Name a method, analysis, dataset, benchmark, or finding. Bind the capability to the evaluated scope.
entries.meaning: States the central contribution and its demonstrated capability in one sentence.

provenance.note: Original reusable pattern authored for this repository.

entries.avoid: Do not imply that a local convention is the field's only accepted definition.
examples: We use {term} to denote {entity or process satisfying explicit conditions}.
entries.expression: We use {term} to denote {operational meaning}.
entries.guidance: Use when the paper needs a definition whose scope is specific to the present formulation. State the defining property, not a circular synonym.
entries.meaning: Introduces a local, operational meaning for a term.

provenance.note: Original reusable pattern authored for this repository.

entries.avoid: Do not use this frame to silently redefine a standard term for rhetorical convenience.
examples: In this work, {term} refers specifically to {property within the studied setting}.
entries.expression: In this work, {term} refers to {scope-bounded definition}.
entries.guidance: Use when community usage is broader than the aspect studied in the paper. Follow with inclusions or exclusions if ambiguity remains.
entries.meaning: Defines a term while making the scope of the definition explicit.

provenance.note: Original reusable pattern authored for this repository.

entries.avoid: Avoid 'we conduct extensive experiments' without stating what questions or settings are evaluated.
examples: We evaluate {method} on {benchmarks} using {metrics} under a matched {budget}.
We evaluate in {simulation or real system} on {tasks}, reporting {metrics} under {protocol}.
entries.expression: We evaluate {method} on {tasks} using {metrics} under {protocol}.
entries.guidance: Name the actual tasks, principal metrics, split or evaluation regime, and any material simulation or deployment condition.
entries.meaning: Introduces the evaluation scope, outcome measures, and protocol in one compact sentence.

provenance.note: Original experimental-writing pattern authored after the section-writing audit.

entries.avoid: Do not select illustrative failures without reporting how frequently they occur in the evaluated population.
examples: Failure cases are dominated by {category}, accounting for {count} of {total} unsuccessful trials.
Among {denominator}, {fraction} involve {condition}; category labels were assigned using {procedure}.
entries.expression: Failure cases are dominated by {category}, accounting for {fraction} of {denominator}.
entries.guidance: Define a mutually interpretable failure taxonomy, label multi-cause cases, and state whether categories were assigned manually or automatically.
entries.meaning: Reports a failure category with its frequency and explicit denominator.

provenance.note: Original results-analysis pattern authored after the section-writing audit.

entries.avoid: Do not call a comparison controlled when data, compute, architecture, or tuning differs materially.
examples: For a controlled comparison, we hold {data and compute budget} fixed and vary only {model component}.
entries.expression: For a controlled comparison, we hold {factor} fixed and vary only {factor}.
entries.guidance: Use only when the protocol truly controls the named factor; list remaining mismatches if they affect interpretation.
entries.meaning: Explains how an experiment isolates a comparison dimension.

provenance.note: Original reusable pattern authored for this repository.

entries.avoid: Do not erase the contribution of the foundational method.
examples: Our formulation builds on {named framework} and extends it to {setting} by {technical modification}.
entries.expression: Our formulation builds on {foundation} and extends it to {new setting or capability}.
entries.guidance: Cite the foundation and explain what changes in the new formulation. Use 'extends' only when the technical relationship is real.
entries.meaning: States intellectual continuity and the precise extension contributed by the paper.

provenance.note: Original reusable pattern authored for this repository.

entries.avoid: Do not write as though the proposed future experiment has already succeeded.
examples: An important next step is to evaluate {capability} under {distribution shift or deployment condition}.
entries.expression: An important next step is to evaluate {capability} under {condition}.
entries.guidance: Use for work not completed in the current paper. Prefer a falsifiable next step over generic aspirations.
entries.meaning: Identifies a concrete unresolved evaluation or research direction.

provenance.note: Original reusable pattern authored for this repository.

entries.avoid: Do not claim that all existing methods fail when only a subset was examined.
examples: Despite progress in {capability}, existing methods remain limited by {assumption or failure mode} in {setting}.
entries.expression: Despite progress in {area}, existing methods remain limited by {specific limitation}.
entries.guidance: The limitation must be supported and relevant to the proposed contribution. Specify the affected regime, assumption, or metric.
entries.meaning: Identifies a research gap without dismissing prior progress.

provenance.note: Original reusable pattern authored for this repository.

entries.avoid: Do not call a test condition unseen if it influenced prompts, hyperparameters, checkpoint selection, or data curation.
examples: The test split holds out {objects} from all training and validation trajectories.
For cross-environment evaluation, {environments} are excluded from both training and model selection.
entries.expression: The {split} holds out {unit} from all training and selection data.
entries.guidance: Name whether the unit is subject, scene, object, task, environment, embodiment, or temporal block. Disclose any preprocessing learned globally.
entries.meaning: Defines a held-out unit and excludes it from both model fitting and selection.

provenance.note: Original experimental-writing pattern authored after the section-writing audit.

entries.avoid: Avoid 'averaged over multiple runs' when the count, independence, and dispersion are not given.
examples: We report the mean and standard deviation over {number} independent seeds.
Values are medians over {number} runs, with {interval} percentiles in parentheses.
entries.expression: We report {statistic} over {number} independent {runs or seeds}.
entries.guidance: Replace the statistical unit precisely and explain nested averaging when episodes or scenes occur within seeds. Name uncertainty separately.
entries.meaning: States the aggregation statistic and number of independent repetitions.

provenance.note: Original experimental-writing pattern authored after the section-writing audit.

entries.avoid: Do not manufacture a taxonomy that collapses technically heterogeneous work or omits the closest method.
examples: Within {task}, the closest approaches can be compared by how they represent {entity} and obtain {supervision}.
Existing methods can be distinguished by {decision mechanism} and {interaction regime}.
entries.expression: Within {scope}, the closest approaches can be compared along {axis one} and {axis two}.
entries.guidance: Choose verified axes such as representation, supervision, data, decision rule, interaction regime, or deployment assumption.
entries.meaning: Organizes related approach families by explicit technical dimensions relevant to the present argument.

provenance.note: Original section-aware pattern authored after the section-writing audit.

entries.avoid: Do not introduce a challenge that no design element or experiment addresses.
examples: The design addresses {challenge} by conditioning {mechanism} on {signal}.
To handle {challenge}, the model uses {technical choice}.
entries.expression: The design addresses {challenge} by {technical choice}.
entries.guidance: Use the same challenge and component names throughout the Introduction, Method, and experiments. Avoid implying causal sufficiency without evidence.
entries.meaning: Maps one emphasized challenge to the corresponding design mechanism.

provenance.note: Original section-aware pattern authored after the section-writing audit.

entries.avoid: Avoid treating the mere number of experiments as a contribution.
examples: We evaluate whether {method} improves {outcome}, transfers across {shift}, and reduces {resource}.
The experiments test {main comparison}, {mechanism claim}, and {deployment boundary}.
entries.expression: Our contributions are evaluated through {research questions}.
entries.guidance: Replace the slot with two or three concrete questions or evaluation axes. Pair non-empirical contributions with theorems, resources, or analyses instead.
entries.meaning: Frames empirical contributions as questions that the Experiments section is designed to answer.

provenance.note: Original section-aware pattern authored after the section-writing audit.

entries.avoid: Do not use a non-goal to dismiss a comparison or safety issue that is essential to the central claim.
examples: We focus on {evaluated setting}; transfer to {unseen setting} remains outside the present study.
Our analysis concerns {formal regime} and does not establish {broader guarantee}.
entries.expression: We focus on {scope}; {non-goal} remains outside the present study.
entries.guidance: Use for a material assumption or non-goal, especially when motivation is broader than evaluation. Keep it consistent with Limitations.
entries.meaning: States an explicit boundary that prevents an overbroad reading of the contribution.

provenance.note: Original section-aware pattern authored after the section-writing audit.

entries.avoid: Avoid using the transition when the design choice is unrelated to the preceding limitation.
examples: Motivated by this observation, we design {mechanism} to preserve {property}.
This analysis motivates {design choice}, which targets {failure mode}.
entries.expression: Motivated by this observation, we design {mechanism} to {goal}.
entries.guidance: Ensure the antecedent observation directly motivates the mechanism. Name the technical goal rather than 'better performance.'
entries.meaning: Bridges a stated insight or empirical observation to the paper's design response.

provenance.note: Original section-aware pattern authored after the section-writing audit.

entries.avoid: Avoid beginning from an expansive societal claim when the paper evaluates a narrower technical setting.
examples: This work studies {task} under {observation and action constraints}.
We consider {task} in the {offline, online, simulated, or real-system} setting.
entries.expression: This work studies {task} under {operational setting}.
entries.guidance: Specify the decision, observation, data, interaction, or deployment regime that makes the task operationally distinct.
entries.meaning: Defines the paper's task and setting before broader motivation or method details.

provenance.note: Original section-aware pattern authored after the section-writing audit.

entries.avoid: Do not describe a design difference as restrictive without showing why it matters for the task.
examples: This assumption becomes restrictive when {shift}, because {technical consequence}.
The requirement for {resource} limits deployment in {setting}, where {constraint}.
entries.expression: This assumption becomes restrictive when {condition}, because {consequence}.
entries.guidance: State the assumption, triggering condition, and consequence explicitly. Support literature and empirical claims with primary evidence.
entries.meaning: Connects a verified method assumption to the condition under which it limits the target capability.

provenance.note: Original section-aware pattern authored after the section-writing audit.

entries.avoid: Do not compare latency across hardware or confuse batched throughput with single-sample latency.
examples: Latency is measured on {hardware} at {precision} and batch size {value}, including {timing boundary}.
End-to-end control latency includes {components} and is averaged over {repetitions} after {warm-up}.
entries.expression: Latency is measured on {hardware} with {precision, batch, and timing boundary}.
entries.guidance: State warm-up, synchronization, repeats, input shape, preprocessing, action decoding, and whether the value is model-only or end to end.
entries.meaning: Defines the hardware and measurement boundary required to interpret latency.

provenance.note: Original experimental-writing pattern authored after the section-writing audit.

entries.avoid: Do not turn a limitation into an unsupported claim that future work will certainly solve it.
examples: Our evaluation is limited to {tasks or environments}; robustness to {shift} remains to be established.
entries.expression: Our evaluation is limited to {scope}; performance under {unseen condition} remains to be established.
entries.guidance: Name the missing population, environment, scale, horizon, embodiment, or distribution. Do not bury a material limitation.
entries.meaning: States an evaluation boundary and separates tested from untested conditions.

provenance.note: Original reusable pattern authored for this repository.

entries.avoid: Do not let readers infer whether a metric is a percentage, fraction, count, error, or normalized score.
examples: Higher values of {metric} indicate {capability}; results are averaged over {tasks} and then over {seeds}.
Lower {metric} indicates {meaning}; each value is averaged over {evaluation unit}.
entries.expression: Higher values of {metric} indicate {meaning}; results are averaged over {unit}.
entries.guidance: Use 'lower' where appropriate and name whether the unit is task, scene, episode, trial, seed, or example.
entries.meaning: Defines metric direction, interpretation, and the statistical unit used for aggregation.

provenance.note: Original experimental-writing pattern authored after the section-writing audit.

entries.avoid: Avoid an empty claim such as 'This is a very challenging problem.'
examples: A central challenge is to {achieve capability} while {respecting data, compute, safety, or deployment constraint}.
entries.expression: A central challenge is to {objective} while {constraint}.
entries.guidance: Name both the desired capability and the condition that makes it difficult. Prefer measurable constraints over adjectives such as challenging or complex.
entries.meaning: Motivates a problem through a concrete objective–constraint tension.

provenance.note: Original reusable pattern authored for this repository.

entries.avoid: Do not invent a taxonomy whose categories overlap without explanation.
examples: Prior approaches differ primarily in how they {technical axis one} and whether they {technical axis two}.
entries.expression: Prior approaches differ primarily in {axis one} and {axis two}.
entries.guidance: Choose axes that expose meaningful assumptions or design choices, then place representative methods along them with citations.
entries.meaning: Organizes related work by technical comparison axes instead of paper-by-paper chronology.

provenance.note: Original reusable pattern authored for this repository.

entries.avoid: Avoid claiming complete novelty merely because the exact combination has not appeared.
examples: Our setting is most closely related to {method family}, but differs in its assumption of {assumption} and its objective of {objective}.
entries.expression: Our setting is most closely related to {family}, but differs in {assumption or objective}.
entries.guidance: Name the closest family before the distinction. The difference should be technically consequential, not cosmetic.
entries.meaning: Positions the present work relative to the nearest literature family.

provenance.note: Original reusable pattern authored for this repository.

entries.avoid: Avoid 'significant' unless statistical significance was actually tested.
examples: {method} improves mean {metric} by {absolute or relative value} over {baseline} under the {protocol} protocol.
entries.expression: {method} improves {metric} by {value} relative to {baseline} under {protocol}.
entries.guidance: State whether the value is absolute or relative, and match the aggregation and uncertainty used in the table.
entries.meaning: Reports a quantified comparison with its baseline and protocol.

provenance.note: Original reusable pattern authored for this repository.

entries.avoid: Do not report a success percentage without the number and composition of physical trials.
examples: Each real-robot task is evaluated in {trials} trials, with success defined as {terminal condition}.
We conduct {number} trials per {task and object} pair and count an intervention as {outcome}.
entries.expression: Each real-system condition is evaluated in {trials} trials, with success defined as {criterion}.
entries.guidance: Also state reset procedure, intervention policy, trial independence, task allocation, and the denominator used for success rate.
entries.meaning: Defines the trial count and success criterion for a physical or deployed-system evaluation.

provenance.note: Original experimental-writing pattern authored after the section-writing audit.

entries.avoid: Do not say 'we agree' and then dismiss the concern without engaging it.
examples: We agree that {evaluation dimension} is important; our current evidence addresses {specific subset}, while {uncovered condition} remains outside scope.
entries.expression: We agree that {concern} is important; our current evidence addresses {covered scope}.
entries.guidance: Use when the concern is valid but broader than the submitted evidence. State the uncovered portion explicitly if space permits.
entries.meaning: Acknowledges a valid concern while delimiting what the current paper can support.

provenance.note: Original reusable pattern authored for this repository.

entries.avoid: Do not begin with a long thank-you paragraph that delays the answer.
examples: Yes. {claim bounded to the question}; the supporting evidence is reported in {table, figure, section, or verified result}.
entries.expression: Yes. {direct answer}; the supporting evidence is {evidence pointer}.
entries.guidance: Use when the answer is genuinely yes. Replace the first token with 'No' or a qualified answer when appropriate; never force agreement.
entries.meaning: Answers a reviewer question immediately and then points to evidence.

provenance.note: Original reusable pattern authored for this repository.

entries.avoid: Do not blame the reviewer for a misunderstanding caused by unclear writing.
examples: We apologize for the ambiguity: {term or claim} refers to {precise scope}, not {plausible alternative reading}.
entries.expression: We apologize for the ambiguity: {precise clarification}.
entries.guidance: Use only when the manuscript wording could reasonably cause the misunderstanding. Follow with the exact revision.
entries.meaning: Acknowledges unclear presentation and states the intended meaning directly.

provenance.note: Original reusable pattern authored for this repository.

entries.avoid: Do not minimize a limitation that invalidates the main claim.
examples: This is a limitation of the current study, but it does not affect our conclusion about {claim within tested scope} because {reason}.
entries.expression: This is a limitation of the current study, but it does not affect {narrower conclusion}.
entries.guidance: Use only when the narrower conclusion truly survives the limitation. Explain why with evidence or logic.
entries.meaning: Makes a bounded concession while preserving a conclusion supported by existing evidence.

provenance.note: Original reusable pattern authored for this repository.

entries.avoid: Do not use a cosmetic correction frame when the issue invalidates the main analysis.
examples: The reviewer is correct that {quantity or label} was stated incorrectly; we will replace it with {correct value} in {location}.
The reviewer is correct that our wording implied {overbroad claim}; we will narrow it to {supported scope}.
entries.expression: The reviewer is correct that {specific statement}; we will correct {location} accordingly.
entries.guidance: Name the exact error, give the corrected statement, and reassess any downstream conclusion that depends on it.
entries.meaning: Accepts a concrete factual or presentation error without conceding claims that are unaffected by it.

provenance.note: Original rebuttal pattern authored for this repository.

entries.avoid: Do not invent a table location or imply that an indirect analysis answers the request.
examples: The requested comparison is already included in {Table or Appendix}, where {method} achieves {verified metric} under {protocol}.
entries.expression: The requested comparison is already included in {location}, where {verified result}.
entries.guidance: Give an exact manuscript location and reproduce numbers faithfully. If absent, use a revision or limitation frame instead.
entries.meaning: Points a reviewer to existing evidence and summarizes only the relevant result.

provenance.note: Original reusable pattern authored for this repository.

entries.avoid: Do not call a comparison budget-matched when only one of several dominant resources is controlled.
examples: At a matched interaction budget of {value}, {method} obtains {metric}, compared with {baseline result}.
When parameter count is matched, the difference in {metric} is {value}.
entries.expression: At a matched {budget}, {method} yields {verified comparison}.
entries.guidance: Name the matched resource and disclose other material differences. Report the exact statistic and uncertainty used in the manuscript.
entries.meaning: Frames a comparison under an explicitly controlled data, interaction, parameter, compute, or tuning budget.

provenance.note: Original reusable comparison pattern authored for this repository.

entries.avoid: Do not imply that an unrun experiment produced a favorable result or promise a result whose outcome is unknown.
examples: We do not currently have evidence for robustness under {shift}; we will restrict the manuscript to the evaluated {scope}.
The requested comparison is not available in the current submission, so we will remove the corresponding general claim.
entries.expression: We do not currently have evidence for {broader claim}; we will restrict the manuscript to {supported claim}.
entries.guidance: Use when the requested experiment was not run or the available analysis is insufficient. Explain what existing evidence still supports.
entries.meaning: Responds to a request that cannot be supported with existing results by narrowing the claim instead of inventing evidence.

provenance.note: Original rebuttal pattern authored for this repository.

entries.avoid: Avoid vague promises such as 'we will improve the paper.'
examples: We will revise {Section or caption} to make {assumption, protocol, or limitation} explicit.
entries.expression: We will revise {location} to make {point} explicit.
entries.guidance: Name the section, statement, figure, caption, or experimental detail and the information to add. Do not promise a new result unless it exists.
entries.meaning: Commits to a concrete presentation change in response to feedback.

provenance.note: Original reusable pattern authored for this repository.

entries.avoid: Do not label directly competing methods as merely complementary to evade comparison.
examples: A complementary line of work studies {adjacent problem}, sharing our interest in {common element} but targeting {different objective}.
entries.expression: A complementary line of work studies {adjacent problem}.
entries.guidance: Explain the relationship after the topic sentence: shared tool, assumption, representation, or evaluation setting.
entries.meaning: Introduces adjacent literature that informs but does not directly solve the same problem.

provenance.note: Original reusable pattern authored for this repository.

entries.avoid: Do not force heterogeneous work into one family merely because papers use similar architectures.
examples: These approaches share the objective of {objective}, but differ in their assumptions about {axis one} and {axis two}.
While both families address {problem}, they obtain supervision from {different sources}.
entries.expression: These approaches share {common objective}, but differ in {technical axes}.
entries.guidance: Support the shared property and each difference with verified citations. Select axes that connect directly to the present method.
entries.meaning: Synthesizes a family of papers through one commonality and one or more technically relevant differences.

provenance.note: Original reusable pattern authored for this repository.

entries.avoid: Avoid a global default statement when several experiments use materially different protocols.
examples: Unless otherwise specified, we report the mean over {number} seeds and use {aggregation rule}.
Unless otherwise specified, all methods use the same {data, compute, or interaction budget}.
entries.expression: Unless otherwise specified, we use {default configuration} in all experiments.
entries.guidance: State the actual default and enumerate consequential exceptions where they occur. Do not use the frame to hide benchmark-specific tuning.
entries.meaning: Declares a shared experimental default while allowing explicitly identified exceptions.

provenance.note: Original reusable pattern authored for this repository.

entries.avoid: Avoid the blanket phrase 'under fair settings' without listing matched and unmatched factors.
examples: All methods use the same {interaction budget}; model size and pretraining data differ as noted in {location}.
Training data are matched across methods, while {baseline} uses {additional resource}.
entries.expression: All methods use the same {resource budget}; remaining differences are {differences}.
entries.guidance: Name data, environment interaction, parameters, training compute, tuning, or evaluation budgets precisely. Do not imply full fairness from one matched resource.
entries.meaning: States one controlled comparison resource while disclosing consequential factors that remain unmatched.

provenance.note: Original experimental-writing pattern authored after the section-writing audit.

entries.avoid: Avoid 'improves by 10%' when readers cannot tell whether this means ten percentage points or ten percent relative.
examples: On {metric}, {method} increases the score from {value} to {value}, a gain of {points} percentage points.
The error decreases from {value} to {value}, corresponding to a {relative value}% relative reduction.
entries.expression: On {metric}, {method} changes {baseline value} to {method value}, an {absolute or relative} difference of {value}.
entries.guidance: For percentages, distinguish percentage-point differences from relative percent changes. Retain the metric unit and aggregation.
entries.meaning: Reports both endpoint values and labels the comparison as absolute or relative.

provenance.note: Original results-analysis pattern authored after the section-writing audit.

entries.avoid: Do not bury a condition that directly contradicts an Abstract or Introduction claim.
examples: Performance degrades under {shift}, which limits the claim to {evaluated range}.
Success falls from {value} to {value} for {condition}; we therefore restrict the conclusion to {scope}.
entries.expression: Performance degrades under {condition}, which limits the claim to {scope}.
entries.guidance: Quantify the degradation, state the denominator, and distinguish a sampled failure condition from a universal boundary.
entries.meaning: Connects an observed failure condition to the boundary it imposes on the paper's claim.

provenance.note: Original results-analysis pattern authored after the section-writing audit.

entries.avoid: Do not select favorable subgroups post hoc without disclosure or ignore degradation elsewhere.
examples: The improvement is concentrated in {long-horizon tasks}, whereas {short-horizon tasks} show comparable performance.
Gains occur primarily under {shift}; in the reference condition, the methods differ by {value}.
entries.expression: The improvement is concentrated in {conditions}, whereas {other conditions} show {outcome}.
entries.guidance: Use subgroup or condition-level results that were defined or transparently labeled exploratory. Report denominators and uncertainty.
entries.meaning: Identifies where an aggregate gain arises and contrasts it with conditions showing a different pattern.

provenance.note: Original results-analysis pattern authored after the section-writing audit.

entries.avoid: Do not call a result consistent when only an average is positive or when important settings reverse the ranking.
examples: The advantage is consistent across {tasks}, except on {task}, where {outcome}.
The direction is stable over {seeds or scales}, although the magnitude varies from {range}.
entries.expression: The advantage is consistent across {settings}, with {exceptions}.
entries.guidance: Name the settings and define consistency using the direction, effect range, uncertainty, or success frequency. Fill the exception slot even if the answer is none observed.
entries.meaning: Summarizes the breadth of an observed comparison while explicitly retaining exceptions.

provenance.note: Original results-analysis pattern authored after the section-writing audit.

entries.avoid: Avoid 'this proves that the gain is due to' when the experiment does not identify the mechanism.
examples: This pattern is consistent with {mechanism}, although differences in {data or scale} are not controlled.
The result suggests {explanation}; however, {alternative} could also account for the change.
entries.expression: This pattern is consistent with {hypothesis}, although {alternative} is not controlled.
entries.guidance: Use after stating the observed result. Replace the slots with a testable hypothesis and a concrete confounder or alternative mechanism.
entries.meaning: Offers a mechanism interpretation while acknowledging a plausible uncontrolled explanation.

provenance.note: Original results-analysis pattern authored after the section-writing audit.

entries.avoid: Do not interpret a non-significant or noisy difference as proof that methods are identical.
examples: We observe no consistent advantage on {tasks}; differences vary in sign across {seeds}.
The estimate differs by {value}, with a {confidence interval} that includes {reference}.
entries.expression: We observe no consistent advantage on {scope}; the difference remains within {uncertainty}.
entries.guidance: Name the uncertainty statistic and comparison scope. If equivalence matters, use an appropriate equivalence or non-inferiority design.
entries.meaning: Reports a null or unstable comparison without converting it into evidence of equivalence.

provenance.note: Original results-analysis pattern authored after the section-writing audit.

entries.avoid: Do not hide the cost in a footnote while presenting the gain as unqualified superiority.
examples: This gain comes with {latency increase}, revealing a trade-off between {accuracy} and {deployment speed}.
Improved robustness is accompanied by {reference-condition change}, indicating a trade-off across {axes}.
entries.expression: This gain comes with {cost}, revealing a trade-off between {axes}.
entries.guidance: Quantify both axes under the same protocol and avoid causal language if the trade-off is only observational.
entries.meaning: Reports a measured benefit together with the resource, quality, safety, or robustness cost that accompanies it.

provenance.note: Original results-analysis pattern authored after the section-writing audit.

entries.avoid: Do not call a method stable from one run or from low variation over correlated evaluation episodes.
examples: Variation across seeds is {standard deviation}, indicating that the ranking is {stable or uncertain} under this protocol.
The interval across trials is {range}, so the observed difference should be interpreted as {bounded conclusion}.
entries.expression: Variation across {seeds or trials} is {statistic}, indicating {bounded inference}.
entries.guidance: Name standard deviation, interquartile range, confidence interval, or another appropriate statistic and keep the inference modest.
entries.meaning: Uses a named variability statistic to qualify the stability of an empirical result.

provenance.note: Original results-analysis pattern authored after the section-writing audit.

entries.avoid: Avoid rhetorical or accusatory questions and compound questions that bundle several requests into one.
examples: Could the authors report the number of random seeds and the dispersion statistic used in Table {n}? This would clarify how stable the reported gains are.
Could the authors state the training budget per method? This would clarify whether the comparison is matched.
entries.expression: Could the authors report {specific quantity or protocol detail}? This would clarify {stated concern}.
entries.guidance: Target quantities recoverable from a standard experimental log or manuscript revision. One question per missing item, phrased neutrally.
entries.meaning: Asks the authors for one concrete, answerable item and states what the answer would resolve.

provenance.note: Original peer-review pattern authored for this repository from community reviewing norms.

entries.avoid: Do not introduce comparisons, claims, or scores absent from the review body, and do not let polish or novelty language substitute for the listed evidence.
examples: Given the clear formulation and strong results on {covered settings}, balanced against the missing {analysis}, the current evidence supports a cautiously positive assessment.
The contribution is well motivated, but until {unresolved item} is addressed the empirical claim remains partially supported.
entries.expression: Given {listed strengths} and {unresolved weaknesses}, the current evidence supports {bounded judgment}.
entries.guidance: Weigh only items already established in the review body. Match the hedging strength to the evidence: firm where results are clear, open where reporting is incomplete.
entries.meaning: Closes a review with an overall judgment that traces explicitly to the listed strengths and weaknesses and no further.

provenance.note: Original peer-review pattern authored for this repository from community reviewing norms.

entries.avoid: Do not present a disclosed limitation as hidden, and do not imply concealment when the manuscript states the assumption.
examples: The authors already acknowledge the fixed-viewpoint assumption and quantify its cost; the open question is how the degradation scales with viewpoint change.
The single-embodiment scope is disclosed in the limitations section; the remaining concern is whether the claimed mechanism depends on it.
entries.expression: The authors already acknowledge {limitation} in {location}; the open question is {boundary probe}.
entries.guidance: Check the limitations section and experimental caveats before writing a weakness. If the point is disclosed, engage with its measured extent instead of presenting it as a discovery.
entries.meaning: Credits a limitation the submission itself discloses before probing its boundary, keeping the review fair to the authors' own reporting.

provenance.note: Original peer-review pattern authored for this repository from community reviewing norms.

entries.avoid: Do not assert properties the review packet cannot verify, such as reproducibility or hidden results, and do not restate a disagreement as a factual error.
examples: The generalization claim rests on results from {evaluated conditions}, which support robustness within that range but not the broader statement in the abstract.
The comparison covers {included baselines}, which establishes progress over those methods but not the field-wide claim.
entries.expression: The {claim} rests on {reported evidence}, which supports {narrower statement} but not {claimed scope}.
entries.guidance: Quote or locate the specific claim and the specific evidence before judging the gap. Keep the weakness about the submission's content, not about unverifiable properties.
entries.meaning: States a review weakness by anchoring it to what the submission actually reports, separating the claim from the evidence behind it.

provenance.note: Original peer-review pattern authored for this repository from community reviewing norms.

entries.avoid: Do not hold a resolved concern open without a reason, and do not flip the overall stance on points the response never addressed.
examples: The added multi-seed run addresses the stability concern; the missing baseline comparison stands, although the stated incompatibility is a reasonable ground.
The clarified protocol resolves the comparability question; the scope concern stands because the new results remain within the original benchmark.
entries.expression: The added {evidence} addresses {original concern}; {remaining concern} stands because {reason}.
entries.guidance: Concede addressed points plainly and separately from unresolved ones. Accept or keep open each remaining concern with a stated reason; do not add demands absent from the original review.
entries.meaning: Updates a review after the author response by explicitly closing concerns the new evidence resolves and restating the ones it does not.

provenance.note: Original peer-review pattern authored for this repository from community reviewing norms.

entries.avoid: Do not generalize beyond the evaluated settings or omit exceptions.
examples: Across {tasks or datasets}, {method} consistently improves {metric} over {named comparison set}.
entries.expression: Under {evaluated setting}, {method} consistently {measured outcome}.
entries.guidance: Use 'consistently' only when the pattern holds across the stated units. Name seeds, tasks, datasets, or metrics as appropriate.
entries.meaning: Reports a recurring empirical pattern with an explicit evaluation boundary.

provenance.note: Original reusable pattern authored for this repository.

entries.avoid: Avoid a transition that merely repeats the distinction.
examples: This distinction matters because it determines whether {downstream consequence}.
entries.expression: This distinction matters because {consequence}.
entries.guidance: Use after defining two concepts or settings. The consequence should be explicit and locally relevant.
entries.meaning: Connects a technical distinction to its consequence for the argument or evaluation.

provenance.note: Original reusable pattern authored for this repository.

entries.avoid: Do not upgrade a qualified Chinese claim into an unconditional English conclusion.
examples: Although {method} improves {metric} on {subset}, the difference is not statistically significant across {units}.
entries.expression: Although {qualified premise}, {bounded conclusion}.
entries.guidance: Keep negation, modality, comparison direction, quantities, and citations attached to the same propositions as in the source.
entries.meaning: Preserves a concession and its qualification during Chinese-to-English reconstruction.

provenance.note: Original reusable pattern authored for this repository.

entries.avoid: Do not report test-optimal settings as if they were selected without access to test results.
examples: Hyperparameters are selected on {validation tasks} using {metric}, and the selected configuration is fixed for all test tasks.
We select the checkpoint with the highest {validation metric} before evaluating it once on {test set}.
entries.expression: Hyperparameters are selected on {validation set} using {criterion}.
entries.guidance: State whether one configuration is shared across tasks and whether test or shifted conditions influenced selection.
entries.meaning: Declares which data and objective selected hyperparameters or checkpoints.

provenance.note: Original experimental-writing pattern authored after the section-writing audit.

entries.avoid: Do not credit an unspecified inductive bias for empirical gains, and do not present a bias as universally helpful without noting the tasks where its assumption fails.
examples: {Architecture choice} encodes an inductive bias toward {assumed structure}, improving {metric} in {regime}.
Ablating {bias source} isolates its contribution to {sample-efficiency or transfer result}.
entries.expression: inductive bias
entries.guidance: Name the bias concretely (architecture, symmetry, prior connectivity, or objective structure), state the assumption it encodes about the task, and support claimed benefits with sample-efficiency, transfer, or ablation evidence rather than intuition.
entries.meaning: A structural assumption built into an architecture, objective, or algorithm that restricts or prefers certain solutions before observing data, shaping what is learned and how much experience is required.

provenance.note: Independent paraphrase of architectural priors for embodied control; no source sentence copied.

entries.avoid: Avoid 'the experiments prove the effectiveness and superiority of our method.'
examples: Across {tasks}, {method} improves {metric} over {baselines} under a matched {budget}.
The ablation supports the contribution of {component} to {measured outcome} in {setting}.
entries.expression: replace vague effectiveness claims with the observed outcome
entries.guidance: Write the measured change directly. Use 'supports the effectiveness of' only when several results jointly justify the scoped judgment; use 'proves' only for a formal result.
entries.meaning: An effectiveness claim is informative only when it names the intervention, comparison, metric, and evaluated setting.

provenance.note: Original usage guidance authored for this repository.

entries.avoid: Do not infer broad out-of-distribution generalization from a random train–test split over nearly identical samples.
examples: We evaluate generalization to unseen {objects or tasks} by holding out {unit} during training.
The current study does not establish transfer across unseen {embodiments or environments}.
entries.expression: name the generalization axis and held-out unit
entries.guidance: State what was held out during training and what unit is averaged at evaluation. Prefer 'generalization to unseen objects' over an unqualified 'generalization ability.'
entries.meaning: Generalization is always relative to a specified shift, such as unseen objects, tasks, environments, users, embodiments, or combinations.

provenance.note: Original cross-domain usage guidance authored for this repository.

entries.avoid: Do not encode unavailable, failed, and zero-valued results with the same blank cell or dash.
examples: A dash denotes a result that was not reported; N/A indicates that the metric is not applicable.
Zero is reported numerically, while failed runs are counted under {failure policy}.
entries.expression: A dash denotes an unreported value, not a measured zero.
entries.guidance: Define every symbol in the caption or footnote. Use 0 or 0.0 only for a measured zero and N/A only when the metric or condition does not apply.
entries.meaning: Separates missing or unreported results from numeric zero and from conditions that are not applicable.

provenance.note: Original table-reporting guidance authored after the section-writing audit.

entries.avoid: Do not translate 可能 or 表明 into an unqualified 'proves', or assume that any two evidential verbs have a context-free ordering.
examples: The results suggest that {hypothesis}, but do not establish {stronger causal claim}.
entries.expression: Distinguish possibility, interpretation, empirical evidence, and formal proof.
entries.guidance: Use 'may/might' for possibility, 'suggests/supports' for a tentative interpretation or evidence relation, 'shows/demonstrates' for a result established within the study design, and 'proves' only for a formal proof under stated assumptions.
entries.meaning: Modal verbs and evidential verbs serve different functions rather than forming one universal strength ordering.

provenance.note: Original usage guidance authored for this repository.

entries.avoid: Avoid mechanically translating 性能 into 'performances' or writing 'achieve better performances' without a metric.
examples: {method} improves performance on {benchmark}, as measured by {metric}.
The methods exhibit different performance profiles across {task groups}.
entries.expression: performance is usually a mass noun when reporting an aggregate result
entries.guidance: Prefer 'improves performance,' 'achieves higher task success,' or the exact metric. Use a plural only when the sentence explicitly distinguishes multiple kinds of performance.
entries.meaning: In empirical writing, 'performance' usually denotes aggregate measured behavior, whereas plural 'performances' is reserved for genuinely distinct acts or types of performance.

provenance.note: Original usage guidance authored for this repository.

entries.avoid: Avoid using 'respectively' when one item maps to several values or when the antecedent order is unclear.
examples: The {first method} and {second method} obtain {first value} and {second value}, respectively.
We use {value one} for {setting one} and {value two} for {setting two}.
entries.expression: respectively requires an unambiguous one-to-one ordering
entries.guidance: Place 'respectively' close to the second list. If the mapping could be misread, split the sentence or state each pairing explicitly.
entries.meaning: Respectively maps two or more ordered lists element by element and should be used only when both lists have matching cardinality and a clear order.

provenance.note: Original usage guidance authored for this repository.

entries.avoid: Do not convert an omission into an accusation, and do not state unverifiable properties, such as reproducibility or hidden failures, as established facts.
examples: No episode counts are reported (absent), so we request them; we cannot judge reproducibility from the packet (unverifiable), so we do not assert it.
The abstract claims real-world generalization while all experiments are simulated (contradicted), which is a claim-evidence mismatch rather than misconduct.
entries.expression: absent from the manuscript versus contradicted by the manuscript versus unverifiable from the manuscript
entries.guidance: Choose the status explicitly before writing the criticism: request what is absent, correct what is contradicted, and mark what is unverifiable as outside the review's evidence rather than asserting it.
entries.meaning: Reviewer statements about a submission carry three distinct evidential statuses: the manuscript omits something, the manuscript contradicts something, or the review packet cannot establish something either way.

provenance.note: Original peer-review pattern authored for this repository from community reviewing norms.

entries.avoid: Do not infer statistical significance from a visibly larger mean, non-overlapping point estimates, or the Chinese adjective 显著 alone.
examples: {method} yields a {value}-point improvement, but the difference is not statistically significant under {test}.
The improvement is substantial relative to {reference scale}, with an effect size of {value}.
entries.expression: statistically significant versus substantial improvement
entries.guidance: Translate 显著 according to evidence: use 'statistically significant' only when a specified statistical analysis supports it; otherwise report the effect size or use a magnitude term justified by context.
entries.meaning: Statistical significance refers to an inferential test or interval criterion, whereas substantial, marked, or large describes effect magnitude and requires a stated scale.

provenance.note: Original usage guidance authored for this repository.

entries.avoid: Never use 'state-of-the-art' as a general adjective for the method or as a synonym for strong.
examples: Under the {protocol} protocol, {method} achieves the best reported {metric} among {comparison set}.
entries.expression: state-of-the-art performance on {benchmark} under {protocol}
entries.guidance: Use only after checking the benchmark, metric, split, protocol, contemporaneous comparison set, and direction of improvement. Prefer the exact result when the scope is narrow.
entries.meaning: A scoped claim that a verified result is best within a defined comparison set.

provenance.note: Original usage guidance authored for this repository.

entries.avoid: Do not claim that every pessimistic penalty provides a valid lower bound.
examples: The objective regularizes Q-values for out-of-distribution actions while fitting Bellman targets on dataset transitions.
Conservative value estimation mitigates {specified offline optimization failure}.
entries.expression: conservative Q-function learning
entries.guidance: Describe the exact regularizer and theoretical or empirical property established by the cited method; conservative bias can trade off underestimation and robustness.
entries.meaning: Learning value estimates with an objective that penalizes overly high Q-values, especially for actions not supported by the offline dataset.

provenance.note: Independent synthesis of linked primary sources; no source sentence copied.

entries.avoid: Do not use 'distribution shift' without naming the two distributions being compared.
examples: Offline policy optimization can induce distribution shift by assigning probability to actions poorly covered by the dataset.
We regularize {policy or value estimate} toward the support of the behavior data.
entries.expression: distribution shift in offline RL
entries.guidance: Specify whether the shift concerns states, actions, transitions, tasks, or observations. Connect the failure mode to bootstrapping or policy optimization when applicable.
entries.meaning: A mismatch between state–action distributions represented in a fixed dataset and those induced by the learned policy, which makes value estimates for unsupported actions unreliable.

provenance.note: Independent synthesis of linked primary sources; no source sentence copied.

entries.avoid: Do not call training from a continually growing replay buffer offline RL.
examples: We consider the offline RL setting, where the agent learns from a fixed dataset {D} and cannot collect additional transitions.
The dataset contains trajectories generated by {behavior policy mixture}.
entries.expression: offline reinforcement learning
entries.guidance: Describe dataset coverage, behavior policies if known, reward availability, and evaluation protocol. Distinguish offline RL from off-policy online learning and imitation learning.
entries.meaning: Reinforcement learning from a fixed dataset of previously collected transitions, without additional environment interaction during training.

provenance.note: Independent synthesis of linked primary sources; no source sentence copied.

entries.avoid: Do not describe supervised imitation from a fixed dataset as reinforcement learning unless a reward-based objective or RL update is used.
examples: We formulate {task} as reinforcement learning, where the agent observes {observation}, selects {action}, and receives {reward}.
The objective is to maximize the expected discounted return under {environment distribution}.
entries.expression: reinforcement learning (RL)
entries.guidance: Specify observation/state, action, reward, horizon or discount, and whether training is online or offline when these choices matter.
entries.meaning: A decision-making framework in which an agent interacts with an environment and learns behavior to maximize expected cumulative reward.

provenance.note: Independent synthesis of linked primary sources; no source sentence copied.

entries.avoid: Do not compare results taken from incompatible protocols without a caveat.
examples: We compare methods at matched environment-interaction budgets and report performance over {number} seeds using {aggregation}.
Because {prior result} uses a different data budget, we report it separately rather than treating it as a controlled baseline.
entries.expression: RL methods should be compared at matched interaction, data, and evaluation budgets.
entries.guidance: Report environment steps, dataset size, number of seeds, evaluation episodes, compute where relevant, and tuning access. Separate final performance from sample efficiency.
entries.meaning: Frames a fair reinforcement-learning comparison around the budgets that determine efficiency and performance.

provenance.note: Independent synthesis of linked primary sources; example wording is original.

entries.avoid: Do not call a value function or open-loop action sequence a policy.
examples: The stochastic policy {symbol} maps {observation or state} to a distribution over {actions}.
We condition the policy on {goal specification} in addition to {observation}.
entries.expression: policy
entries.guidance: Use π(a|s) for a stochastic policy and state whether conditioning is on state, observation, goal, language, or history.
entries.meaning: A rule or conditional distribution that maps an agent's information state, such as an observation or history, to actions.

provenance.note: Canonical term indexed from linked primary papers; examples are original.

entries.avoid: Do not infer sample efficiency from wall-clock speed or final performance alone.
examples: We evaluate sample efficiency by comparing {metric} after {matched number} environment steps.
The method reaches {performance threshold} using {data amount}.
entries.expression: sample efficiency / data efficiency
entries.guidance: Name the sample unit—steps, episodes, demonstrations, images, or hours—and compare learning curves or performance at matched data budgets.
entries.meaning: The amount of environment interaction or training data required to reach a specified level of performance.

provenance.note: Canonical term indexed from linked primary papers; examples are original.

entries.avoid: Do not infer overestimation solely because a policy performs poorly.
examples: The critic overestimates values for actions outside the dataset support.
We measure value overestimation by comparing {predicted quantity} with {reference return}.
entries.expression: value overestimation
entries.guidance: Identify the estimator and distribution on which overestimation is measured. In offline RL, relate it to actions not well supported by data when justified.
entries.meaning: Systematic upward bias in estimated values, often amplified when optimization selects actions whose estimates are erroneously high.

provenance.note: Canonical term indexed from linked primary papers; examples are original.

entries.avoid: Do not equate off-policy with offline: off-policy training may still collect new environment data.
examples: The algorithm is off-policy and reuses transitions from {replay buffer or fixed dataset}.
Unlike on-policy updates, the critic can learn from data collected by {behavior policy}.
entries.expression: on-policy versus off-policy learning
entries.guidance: Describe the actual behavior and target policies, correction mechanism, and data reuse. Finite policy lag is an implementation approximation whose effect depends on the algorithm; recency alone does not make data on-policy.
entries.meaning: On-policy updates estimate or optimize the target policy using data generated by that same policy, whereas off-policy methods can learn about a target policy from data generated by a different behavior policy.

provenance.note: Independent synthesis of linked primary sources; no source sentence copied.

entries.avoid: Do not treat an interpretable-looking intermediate output as causal evidence that the policy used the stated reasoning process.
examples: The model predicts {affordance representation} as an intermediate target before decoding {robot action}.
entries.expression: chain-of-affordance reasoning
entries.guidance: State the intermediate representation, its supervision, and whether it is generated explicitly at inference time.
entries.meaning: An intermediate reasoning formulation that decomposes a manipulation instruction into action-relevant object, spatial, or interaction affordances before control prediction.

provenance.note: Synthesis of recent affordance- and chain-of-thought-conditioned VLA formulations.

entries.avoid: Do not use this term as a synonym for the entire policy or assume that a continuous head eliminates temporal discretization.
examples: The continuous action head maps {fused representation} to {horizon} steps of {action parameterization}.
entries.expression: continuous action head
entries.guidance: Specify the distribution or regression objective, action parameterization, prediction horizon, and embodiment-specific output dimensions.
entries.meaning: A policy output module that directly parameterizes continuous robot controls rather than representing every action dimension as a discrete language token.

provenance.note: Scope-bounded synthesis of continuous action prediction in recent VLA work.

entries.avoid: Do not rank systems across unmatched robots, demonstrations, tasks, or evaluation protocols.
examples: Existing VLA systems differ in whether they {backbone adaptation}, represent actions as {representation}, learn from {supervision}, and execute under {feedback regime}.
entries.expression: VLA systems should be compared by backbone adaptation, action representation, supervision, and feedback regime.
